Subtracted an extra 90°.

solution: The angles at a point add up to 360°. The reflex angle is the rest of the full turn.

questions.stem: Xin Yi wants to draw ∠PQR = 35°, with QP along the baseline of the protractor pointing to the left. Xin Yi marks R at 35 on the outer scale (the scale that starts at 0 on the right). What is the actual size of ∠PQR in the drawing?

explain.why: Was one 10° interval out.
Took the outer scale reading as the angle even though QP is not on its 0°.
Was one 10° interval out.

solution: QP is on the left, so the 0° mark for this angle is on the left.
The mark R is at 35 on the outer scale, so on the other scale it reads 180° - 35° = 145°.

explain.why: Took the inner scale reading as the angle even though QP is not on its 0°.
Was one 10° interval out.
Was one 10° interval out.

solution: QP is on the right, so the 0° mark for this angle is on the right.
The mark R is at 115 on the inner scale, so on the other scale it reads 180° - 115° = 65°.

Half pass through opposite vertices, the other half through midpoints of opposite sides: 4 ÷ 2 = 2

questions.stem: Mei Ling cuts out these shapes: rectangle, hexagon, square, pentagon, octagon, square, square. How many of them have exactly 4 sides?

explain.why: Miscounted.
Counted one extra.
Counted the shapes that do not fit.

solution: Sides: triangle 3, square 4, rectangle 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6, octagon 8.

explain.why: Multiplied 4 by n only.
Gave the number of squares.
Cut each square into 2 triangles.

questions.stem: Kumar copies the figure on a dot grid. Which drawing, A to D, is an exact copy of the figure?

explain.why: Drew the mirror image of the figure.
Drew the figure turned a quarter-turn.
Changed the length of one side when copying.

solution: A copy has the same shape, the same side lengths and faces the same way.
Drawing A matches the figure side for side.

questions.stem: Nurul cuts out these shapes: octagon, triangle, rectangle, rectangle, rectangle, pentagon, square. How many of them have more than 4 sides?

explain.why: Missed one.
Counted the shapes that do not fit.
Counted one extra.

solution: Sides: triangle 3, square 4, rectangle 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6, octagon 8.

questions.stem: Ravi draws the four nets A, B, C and D, each made of 6 squares. How many of them can be folded to make a cube without any overlap or gap?

explain.why: Counted the nets that do not fold into a cube.
Rejected a valid net.
Accepted a net where two faces overlap.

solution: A cube net needs 6 squares that fold with no two faces landing on the same side.
Rows of four squares with one square above and one below always work; a net with four squares in a row and both extras on the same side, or with a 2 × 2 block, fails.

Miscounted.
Accepted a net where two faces overlap.

solution: A cube net needs 6 squares that fold with no two faces landing on the same side.
Rows of four squares with one square above and one below always work; a net with four squares in a row and both extras on the same side, or with a 2 × 2 block, fails.

questions.stem: Xin Yi's prism has 12 edges. How many faces does it have?

explain.why: Stopped at the number of sides of the base.
Used base sides + 1 faces.
Made a slip of 10 in the final subtraction.

solution: Base has n sides: a prism has 3n edges, 2n vertices, n + 2 faces.

Accepted a net where two faces overlap.
Miscounted.

solution: A cube net needs 6 squares that fold with no two faces landing on the same side.

questions.stem: Four nets of six squares are shown. For how many of them will the squares fold up to form a cube? (Daniel is testing them.)

explain.why: Miscounted.
Rejected a valid net.
Accepted a net where two faces overlap.

solution: A cube net needs 6 squares that fold with no two faces landing on the same side.
Rows of four squares with one square above and one below always work; a net with four squares in a row and both extras on the same side, or with a 2 × 2 block, fails.

explain.why: Stopped at the number of sides of the base.
Used base sides + 1 faces.
Made a slip of 10 in the final subtraction.

solution: Base has n sides: a prism has 3n edges, 2n vertices, n + 2 faces.

Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.

questions.stem: A paper strip ZAY is folded along the line AB so that AZ falls on AZ′, as shown by the dotted line. ∠Z′AY = 124°. Find ∠ZAB.

explain.why: Gave the given angle.
Gave the supplement of the answer.
Found ∠ZAZ′ but did not halve it.

solution: A fold is a reflection, so ∠ZAB = ∠Z′AB.

questions.stem: ABCD is a rhombus with ∠ABC = 46°. CDE is an equilateral triangle and A and E are on opposite sides of CD. Find ∠DAE.

explain.why: Found the sum of the base angles but did not halve it.
Found ∠ADE and stopped.
Halved the supplement of ∠ABC (this is ∠CAD, not ∠DAE).

solution: ∠ADE = 46° + 60° = 106° (C is between A and E on the angle at D)
DA = DC = DE, so triangle ADE is isosceles.

Halved the supplement of ∠ABC (this is ∠CAD, not ∠DAE).

DA = DC = DE, so triangle ADE is isosceles.

explain.why: Left out one side.
Added the perimeters of the two shapes, counting the joined side twice.
Made a slip of 10 in the final subtraction.

solution: Total length across the bottom = 6 + 13 = 19 cm
Height of the tall square = 13 cm
The outline goes right and up the same distance as the bounding rectangle: 2 × (19 + 13) = 64 cm

Made a slip of 10 in the final subtraction.
Left out one side.

The outline goes right and up the same distance as the bounding rectangle: 2 × (26 + 11) = 74 cm
